title: Metabolic Integration and Regulation
objectives: Explain how major metabolic pathways interconnect
Analyze metabolic adaptations in fed vs. fasted states

pathway_interconnections.title: Interconnected Metabolic Pathways
pathway_interconnections.content:
Central Metabolic Network

1. Carbohydrate-Lipid-Protein Nexus

  • Glycolysis: Glucose → Pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA (fatty acid synthesis)
  • TCA Cycle: Hub for carbon skeletons (amino acids → energy)
  • Gluconeogenesis: Lactate/amino acids → glucose (liver)

2. Key Shared Metabolites

  • Acetyl-CoA (link between carbs, fats, proteins)
  • Oxaloacetate (TCA ↔ gluconeogenesis)
  • PRPP (nucleotide synthesis)

tissue_specialization.title: Tissue-Specific Metabolism
tissue_specialization.content:
Division of Metabolic Labor

1. Liver

  • Fed state: Glycogenesis, lipogenesis
  • Fasted state: Gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis
  • Detoxification (CYP450)

2. Muscle

  • Glycogen storage: Rapid glucose release
  • Fatty acid oxidation: Energy for sustained activity
  • Creatine phosphate system

3. Adipose Tissue

  • Lipid storage: TAG synthesis (fed state)
  • Lipolysis: FFA release (fasted state)
  • Leptin secretion

4. Brain

  • Primary fuel: Glucose (ketones during starvation)
  • Blood-brain barrier selectivity

hormonal_regulation.title: Hormonal Control
hormonal_regulation.content:
Metabolic Regulators

1. Insulin (Fed State)

  • ↑GLUT4 translocation (glucose uptake)
  • ↑Glycogenesis, lipogenesis
  • ↓Gluconeogenesis, lipolysis

2. Glucagon (Fasted State)

  • ↑Glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis
  • ↑Lipolysis (adipose)
  • ↑Ketogenesis (liver)

3. Cortisol/Epinephrine

  • Cortisol: Chronic stress → protein catabolism
  • Epinephrine: Acute stress → glycogenolysis

fed_fasted_states.title: Fed vs. Fasted States
fed_fasted_states.content:
Metabolic Transitions

1. Postprandial (Fed) State

  • 0-4 hours: Glucose → glycogen (liver/muscle)
  • 4-12 hours: Fatty acid synthesis (liver → adipose)
  • Insulin dominates

2. Fasted State (≥12h)

  • Early: Glycogenolysis → gluconeogenesis
  • Late (≥2 days): Ketogenesis (brain adaptation)
  • Glucagon/cortisol dominate

clinical.title: Clinical Correlations
clinical.content:
Metabolic Disorders

1. Diabetes Mellitus

  • Type 1: Insulin deficiency → unopposed catabolism
  • Type 2: Insulin resistance → dysregulated fed/fasted transitions
  • Lab findings: Hyperglycemia, ketoacidosis (Type 1)

2. Metabolic Syndrome

  • Central obesity + insulin resistance
  • Dyslipidemia (↑TAG, ↓HDL)
  • ↑CVD risk

3. Starvation Adaptation

  • Phase 1: Glycogen depletion (24h)
  • Phase 2: Protein catabolism → gluconeogenesis
  • Phase 3: Ketosis (brain fuel shift)

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
FAQs

Q: Why does the brain prefer glucose? +

A: Neurons lack significant glycogen stores and require ATP for ion pumps. Glucose provides rapid energy via glycolysis and is the only fuel that crosses the BBB under normal conditions (ketones during starvation).

Q: How does insulin resistance disrupt metabolic integration? +

A: Impaired GLUT4 translocation causes persistent postprandial hyperglycemia, while adipose lipolysis continues unchecked → excess FFA delivery to liver → gluconeogenesis + ketogenesis despite high glucose.

Q: Why is acetyl-CoA considered a metabolic hub? +

A> It links: (1) Glycolysis (pyruvate → acetyl-CoA), (2) Fatty acid oxidation (β-oxidation → acetyl-CoA), (3) Amino acid degradation (ketogenic AAs → acetyl-CoA), and (4) TCA cycle (entry via citrate synthase).
